case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports (1978-79-80) 1 Sri. L.R. 102

clause.text: No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner's dismissal was discriminatory on the ground of political opinion in violation of Article 12(2).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that her removal was due to political victimization and discrimination based on her political opinion, contrary to Article 12(2).
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the dismissal was lawful under the Cabinet's constitutional powers, that no intentional or hostile discrimination on political grounds was proven, and that the Cabinet's decision was bona fide to remedy prior political victimization.
key_facts: Petitioner was a member of the Lanka Sama Samaja Party; Indra Ranjini belonged to the United National Party.
Political Victimization Committee recommended cancellation of petitioner's appointment and appointment of Indra Ranjini.
Petitioner was not given a hearing before the Committee; the Committee's proceedings were ex parte.
The Cabinet acted on the Committee's recommendation to terminate petitioner and appoint Indra Ranjini.
No evidence showed that the Cabinet's decision was motivated by hostile or intentional discrimination.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court interpreted Article 12(2) as prohibiting intentional and hostile discrimination on specified grounds including political opinion. Mere errors, breaches of law, or administrative decisions without discriminatory intent do not violate Article 12(2). The Court emphasized the need for proof of purposeful discrimination to establish a breach.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the Cabinet's decision was a bona fide attempt to remedy political victimization and was not tainted by mala fides or hostile discrimination. The petitioner failed to prove that her dismissal was due to discrimination on political grounds under Article 12(2).
principles_established: Discrimination under Article 12(2) requires intentional and hostile unequal treatment.
Administrative or executive errors or breaches of law without discriminatory intent do not violate Article 12(2).
Political victimization claims must be substantiated with evidence of purposeful discrimination.
The Cabinet's wide powers to dismiss public officers are subject to fundamental rights but presumed valid absent proof of discrimination.
precedents_cited: Siddappa v. State of Mysore AIR 1967 (Mysore) 67
Budhan Chowdhary v. State of Bihar AIR 1955 (SC) 191
The State of Jammu & Kashmir v. Ghulam Rasool AIR 1961 (SC) 1301

outcome.holding: The Court dismissed the petitioner's claim under Article 12(2), holding that no discriminatory breach of fundamental rights on political grounds was established.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(2) was directly engaged as the petitioner alleged discrimination on political grounds in her dismissal. The Court's analysis focused on the requirement of intentional discrimination to invoke this fundamental right.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner claimed political victimization and discrimination in her dismissal. The Court found the Cabinet's action was bona fide to remedy prior political victimization and no evidence of hostile or intentional discrimination was shown.
